title: "Put on headphones, follow the instructions, and tour a city": an unusual performance begins
excerpt: Some call it a "deep dive into Xuhui District," but the creators are after much more than that — artificial intelligence, group dynamics — and those philosophical questions are easily drowned out over two hours.
body:
Some call it a "deep dive into Xuhui District," but the creators are after much more than that — artificial intelligence, group dynamics — and those philosophical questions are easily drowned out over two hours.

The starting point is Gate 3 of Longhua Martyrs' Cemetery — that was one of the most important pieces of information I had going into this outdoor promenade performance called *Remote Shanghai*.

Over the next two hours I passed through a cemetery and a temple, rode the subway, and made my way through a shopping mall, a hospital and a pedestrian overpass, ending on a raised platform.

The show has no professional actors, and no staff to guide you. All twenty-odd of us followed the instructions in our headphones, spoken in the flat voice of a GPS navigation system: walk forward, stop, turn around, make a gesture, think about something. It sounds a lot like performance art — and none of us knew what we were in for.

This is the unusual format of *Remote X*, a piece of documentary theater created by the German company Rimini Protokoll. The troupe got its name when its three founders, sitting in a bar, idly lifted a beer coaster and found the word "Rimini" printed underneath.

![A production photo from *Remote Shanghai* (photo by Yin Xuefeng)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011221738peguofdDm0cG2qbH.JPG-w600)

This time Rimini Protokoll co-produced *Remote Shanghai* with the Shanghai Dramatic Arts Center (SDAC), the first mainland Chinese version of the show. Before this, *Remote X* — where X stands for any city — had visited Berlin, Milan, New York, Paris, London, Taipei and others, sometimes with more than one version made for the same city.

The official description this time reads: "Put on headphones, follow the instructions and tour a city; the whole city is a ready-made stage." The literal Chinese for "remote" is *yaokong*, "remote-controlled," but SDAC chose the looser *yaogan*, "remote sensing." The audience is remote-controlled through the city, just as the advance of modern urban life and artificial intelligence has put everything under remote control. On another level, the audience keeps a new distance from the city it lives in, hunting for something fresh inside the familiar.

In what follows I'll try not to give away specific locations or instructions. If this interests you, I hope you have a wonderful experience of your own.

I deliberately skipped the press showing. I wanted to see how ordinary audience members would react, and what a smaller crowd would be like, so I picked the afternoon of October 9th, a weekday (the show starts at the same time, 2 p.m., on weekdays and weekends alike).

More people turned up than I expected — about 25 of us, half the stated 50-person cap. Most of them worked in theater, which is why their schedules were flexible enough for a weekday afternoon. I also met one audience member who works in New York, loves theater, and happened to be back in China on vacation.

![At the October 9th afternoon show, the construction workers behind us became part of the performance too (photo by the reporter)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011221858qWEezX9wt7j8F5VR.jpg-w600)

Since I hadn't brought any valid ID, a friend who came with me paid the 500-yuan deposit on my behalf, and I was handed a set of professional equipment — over-ear headphones and a one-way subway ticket.

Once the headphones were on, I was guided to a patch of green space behind me. Paths crisscrossed the ground, rows of martyrs' headstones stood in neat order, a gardener was trimming the grass, and the smell of cut grass hit me — the first smell I registered. Later there were others, some so pleasant I didn't want to leave, others that made me cover my nose and want to run.

But the voice in the headphones sounded jarring. Once you decide, subjectively, that this is a theatrical performance, you take it for granted that the voice will rise and fall, carry feeling, have charm. This one sounded like the factory setting on a GPS unit.

I talked myself into it right away: one of the things the creators wanted to examine is exactly this, what artificial intelligence does to our lives. The voice seemed to know what I was thinking and answered my questions almost as soon as I had them. This kept happening, and inside the situation I found it delightful. Two days later I'd sobered up — it isn't really "artificial intelligence." Every word of it was scripted by the creators.

![Headphones and a subway ticket (photo by the reporter)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201810112220216iT1UyWuQBDV8YCr.jpg-w600)

Starting at a martyrs' cemetery makes it hard not to think in heavy terms. I assumed the show would have to be about human existence, about life and death, and that the tone would be solemn and profound. It turned out that these two hours, which we took part in rather than watched, departed a long way from what I expected. There were serious stretches, but humor, playful questions, instructions and interaction took up far more of the time.

The trouble with that is the thought-provoking questions flash past. You are quickly on the next stretch of road, laughing again or hurrying to keep up. When I tried afterward to recall the specific questions, I couldn't. They come back as fragments; I want to hold onto the instant, and all that's left is an afterglow. Most of the thinking happened over the following two days, not at the time.

From cemetery to temple, from mall to hospital, from subway to street market — the whole two hours stay inside Shanghai's Xuhui District, which is why some call it a "deep dive into Xuhui District." Fair enough: Xuhui has few landmarks worth checking in at, and the route (which I won't reveal) will feel entirely ordinary to anyone who knows the district.

To me, though, the "Remote" is the more important half. An everyday route carries far less ceremony than a landmark does, and that is exactly what lets you settle down and take it in: What is our life like? Why are we here? Why do we follow instructions? Of course, seeing *Remote X* in a city you don't know would be a completely different experience.

![A production photo from another city's version of *Remote X* (image from the troupe's official website)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011222411UpVLWXJQYGnFbh4S.jpg-w600)

Looking at this familiar setting in the frame of mind of "I am performing" and "I am watching a performance" was endlessly entertaining. The foreign director wrote back to me that finding a different perspective on daily city life is what matters most. One person imagining that walking against the flow of pedestrians is a monster fight is a bit adolescent; a whole group doing it together somehow looks convincing. Which points to the next few questions.

**1. Does the collective really matter that much?**

At the start of the show we were told we were a "tribe": we had to walk together for the signal to be stronger; we would occasionally have to decide which way to go; we had to wait for anyone falling behind; we had to cross the street together, and so on.

For most of the two hours we stayed together, but later our routes diverged under instruction. Some people said goodbye without a second thought; others kept glancing back. The collective clearly means different things to different people, even a temporary one made up mostly of strangers in a theater piece.

Inside that larger collective, I was there with a friend, and the two of us made a smaller one. Having something to lean on made me giddier, not her. Does the "support" of a collective free us to let go? The answer seems to depend entirely on the person.

![A production photo from another city's version of *Remote X* (image from the troupe's official website)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011223353AsNWQT0rOCu1gjfz.jpg-w600)

One small episode, unrelated to the two-hour show itself, also made me think. Arriving early at Gate 3 of the martyrs' cemetery, I saw two audience members waiting there together and instinctively took the spot for the meeting point. My friend saw me stop there and stopped too, and more people joined us afterward. By 2 p.m., the scheduled start, there was still no sign of anything beginning, and I began to wonder whether the show had been canceled for want of an audience — until a staff member came out and directed us another 100 meters inside. That was the real starting point.

If I had been the first to arrive, would I have gone in to look around? I probably would have messaged the staff on WeChat right away. Alone, you're isolated; there's no way to prove "my choice is the right one." It was precisely because others got there first, and I assumed by default that they were right, that I chose to join them. That is how we became a larger collective — and then misled more people in turn. I've always thought of myself as someone who doesn't follow the crowd, but the pull of being one of the group turns out to matter far more than I thought.

![A production photo from *Remote Shanghai* (photo by Yin Xuefeng)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011223831O2FJt84w50P76NVA.JPG-w600)

**2. Do we have to obey the voice in the headphones?**

In principle, yes.

The mechanical voice in the headphones seemed to have anticipated every audience reaction: some people did as they were told, some chose another way — on the condition that the alternative didn't disrupt the show and left nobody behind.

Are the people who ignore instructions smarter? Or lazier? That is what the voice asked me after I broke one of them. That day everyone followed the instructions almost every time; people were more diligent about it than I expected.

Why shouldn't the square-dancing aunties dance with headphones on? Trust me: if you take part in this show, film a short video and watch it back later, you'll see how strange a silent performance looks. One person swaying in headphones is understandable; a whole group of them doing it in a cramped public space is eerie.

Only a few can follow the instructions and stay giddy all the way through. The further you go, the more you start to doubt yourself.

![A production photo from *Remote Shanghai* (photo by Yin Xuefeng)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011223956TzX0dKyCfWu2plO1.JPG-w600)

**3. What does the new relationship between stage and audience look like?**

Every one of us is a performer, every one of us is a spectator, and any passerby can be either. The "fourth wall" is broken from the first minute. Unlike the usual two-sided arrangement, *Remote X* has no stage and no seats. Or, to put it another way, every place we walk through is the stage, and wherever we stand is the seating.

Our collective behavior puts on a show for passersby, and their unwitting participation — even just walking past — is taken apart by the voice in our headphones and rebuilt as performance. The performance leaves no visible trace, and they have no idea they have become the thing we are watching. At the same time, the twenty-some of us form a stage-and-audience relationship among ourselves: when someone answers a question from the voice with a sudden movement of the body, they become a more prominent performer within the group.

![A production photo from *Remote Shanghai* (photo by Yin Xuefeng)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011224442lsxzHAjQ82SY9cR3.JPG-w600)

However hard we "performed" for everyone, though, not many people noticed us. Most were hurrying somewhere or looking down at their phones. Only three or four spots along the route drew an obvious crowd.

At one point we did something wildly unlike ordinary pedestrian behavior, and I saw a woman in her fifties raise her phone toward us. When I got closer, I realized she was probably just adjusting the camera to photograph the flowers behind her. It turns out we were neither as conspicuous nor as important as we imagined.

In a show built on instructions, we were never forbidden from using our phones, so the world we touched came in two layers: the "small world" that connects us to other people through the phone, and the world in front of us that we observed while following the voice. At no point did the show try to build an "illusion theater." Every minute and second of it was real, and that may be the deepest meaning of documentary.

### We spoke with Anton Rose, one of the directors, to learn more.

**Q: Some elements — the cemetery, the mall, the hospital — seem to be required. How do you pick the other locations? Is the temple something specific to mainland China?**

Anton Rose: We have more or less definite requirements for every city, but we're also happy to include special locations. The temple on the Shanghai route is without question a very beautiful and interesting place, but it isn't a temple we deliberately went looking for.

**Q: How do you distinguish "performance art" from "documentary theater"? The format of *Remote X* — acting on instructions — probably looks to a lot of people like collective performance art.**

Anton Rose: *Remote X* does contain both performance art and documentary theater. But for me it's a hybrid, using many elements that are hard to file under any one category.

![A production photo from *Remote Shanghai* (photo by Yin Xuefeng)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011233437DUoJpcY7V9Wz0KCs.JPG-w600)

**Q: Why did you choose a humorous way to take on subjects like artificial intelligence and obeying or defying instructions?**

Anton Rose: Humor matters a great deal to me. It can help us beat boredom and sadness, and sometimes it also helps us understand things, creating a workable distance between us and serious real life.

**Q: You also examine the relationship between the collective and the individual. Have you ever had a performance with only one audience member?**

Anton Rose: I think *Remote X* is about group dynamics, so the group can't be too small. At the same time, I'm very interested in making a show for a single spectator.

**Q: Is it done by GPS positioning, or do staff on site intervene?**

Anton Rose:

All I can say is that it involves technology and some tricks, and of course a lot of hard work.

![A signal receiver (photo by the reporter)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011225106olvrMpN8PKkEST9X.jpg-w600)

**Q: In Berlin, Taipei, Moscow, New York and elsewhere, *Remote X* has more than one version. What's the difference between versions in the same city?**

Anton Rose: In theory any reasonably large city could have two versions or more, but I think in those cities, apart from small changes, the routes are actually the same — meaning they aren't different versions, just more performances. Berlin is the exception: there are two completely different routes there.

![A production photo from the Taipei run of *Remote X* (image from the troupe's [official website](https://www.rimini-protokoll.de/website/en/project/remote-x))](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20181011234017gcwPGhWIvM2Us5Kl.jpg-w600)

**Q: If audiences remember only the lightness and the fun, without thinking hard about the questions you wanted to raise, would you find that a shame?**

Anton Rose: I've personally put a lot of subjects and questions into *Remote X*; they're thought-provoking and they matter. So when I was making this project, my aim was to find an effective way to get people to reflect on them. That said, I still count genuinely making people happy as a very big achievement, so as long as nobody is bored, it isn't too bad.

### Show information

*Remote X*, Shanghai edition

Dates: October 8 – November 4, 2018 (dark on Mondays), 2 p.m., running two hours

Meeting point: inside the Gate 3 entrance of Longhua Martyrs' Cemetery

Tickets: 150 yuan Tuesday to Friday; 200 yuan Saturday and Sunday

Where to buy: the Shanghai Dramatic Arts Center's official Tmall store

Cover image and banner image are both production photos from *Remote Shanghai*, photographed by Yin Xuefeng. The Shanghai-edition photos in the text are provided by the Shanghai Dramatic Arts Center.
